findings.summary: American Fuzzy Lop (AFL) is a free, open-source fuzzer that uses genetic algorithms to maximize code coverage and uncover software bugs. It requires a command to run the target program and an initial input. AFL first minimizes the input, then iteratively mutates it using deterministic bit-flips, integer adjustments, and dictionary-based replacements. After deterministic steps, it applies 'havoc' mutations—random overwrites and block operations—and 'splicing' to combine inputs. The fuzzer tracks coverage via 'binned hitcounts' of control-flow edges, adding new inputs to a queue only when they produce unseen coverage metrics, prioritizing inputs that trigger crashes or hangs.

mechanisms.title: Deterministic and Havoc Mutation
mechanisms.explanation: AFL generates new test cases by first applying a deterministic sequence of bit-flips, integer increments/decrements, and dictionary-based replacements to existing inputs. Once these are exhausted, it performs 'havoc' mutations, overwriting bytes with random values and applying block-level operations like deletion, duplication, and byte-filling. These stages explore the input space systematically before resorting to crossover.

mechanisms.title: Binned Hitcount Coverage Metric
mechanisms.explanation: AFL measures code coverage by counting how often each control-flow edge is traversed during execution. Hitcounts are binned into eight categories (1, 2, 3, 4–7, 8–15, 16–31, 32–127, 128+). A new input is retained in the queue only if it produces a (edge, binned count) pair not previously observed, enabling efficient prioritization of inputs that expand program exploration without computationally expensive trace comparisons.
